a1.say: Let's solve Count the Islands, using the DFS Flood Fill approach.

a1.cap: grid is a map of "1" (land) and "0" (water). An island is land connected up, down, left or right. Return the number of islands. You may modify the grid.

lines: grid is a map of "1" (land) and "0" (water). An island is land connected up, down, left or right. Return the number of islands. You may modify the grid.

a1.cap: Scan every cell. When you hit land, that's a new island: count it, then run a depth-first search that turns the whole connected island into water so it won't be counted again.
New land at row 0, column 0: island number 1.
Sink every cell of this island.
New land at row 1, column 3: island number 2.
Sink every cell of this island.
Time complexity is O(m · n) and extra space is O(m · n). Each cell is sunk at most once; the recursion can go as deep as the island's size.
a1.say: Time complexity is O of m times n and extra space is O of m times n. Each cell is sunk at most once; the recursion can go as deep as the island's size.

a1.cap: That's the DFS Flood Fill approach. Now try writing it yourself, in Java or Python!
